episodes.title: How the Tiger Got His Stripes

subtitle.text: Tiger ruled the jungle.
He had sharp fangs, long claws, and smooth golden fur.
When he roared, everyone trembled with fear.
"Get out of my way!" Tiger roared.
Birds, monkeys, and other small animals scattered.
But Water Buffalo was bigger than Tiger.
"Don't tell me what to do."
Water Buffalo walked right by and dipped into the lake.
"Hmph!" Tiger slashed a tree.
"How can I make him listen to me?"
A week later Tiger was roaming through the jungle.
In one area all the trees were gone.
Suddenly Tiger saw a new animal.
It walked on two legs and cut down weeds.
"Pull the plow!" it commanded another animal.
Tiger gasped. "That's Water Buffalo!
Why is he listening to that weak-looking animal?"
The strange animal walked away.
Tiger hurried over to Water Buffalo.
"What's going on? Who is that?"
"That's a human," Water Buffalo said.
"He's farming the land."
Tiger blinked. "Why do you listen to him?
He's smaller than you. Plus he doesn't have claws or fangs."
"That's true. But he has something more powerful," Water Buffalo said.
"He has wisdom."
Tiger rubbed his chin.
"I need wisdom. Then everyone would listen to me."
Tiger hurried after the human. "Hey!"
The human spun around and trembled with fear.
Tiger snarled. "Give me some wisdom!"
The human gulped. "Okay. But I, um . . ."
A sly grin slowly formed on his face.
"I left it at home."
Tiger snarled again. "Go and get it."
"Yes, sir!" The human started to walk away but then stopped.
He bit his lip.
"You might eat my water buffalo while I'm away.
Perhaps I can tie you to that tree?"
Tiger sighed. "Fine. Just get me that wisdom."
"Of course." The human grabbed a rope.
He wrapped it around Tiger and the tree.
"I'll be right back." The human walked away, whistling.
The blazing sun heated up the rope.
After an hour Tiger groaned.
"That man tricked me."
He tried to break free, but the rope was strong.
For hours he struggled.
The hot rope tightly rubbed against Tiger's fur, growing hotter.
Smoke rose, and the smell of burning fur filled Tiger's nose.
"Roar!" Finally Tiger broke free and darted to the lake.
Then he saw his reflection. His fur was burnt!
"I have stripes!" Tiger frowned.
"But I did get some wisdom after all.
Now I know not to trust humans!"

episodes.title: Why the Bear Has a Stumpy Tail

subtitle.text: Long ago Bear had a beautiful tail.
It was long and fluffy and kept him warm while he slept.
But one day everything changed.
Bear ran into a sneaky fox.
And this fox liked to play tricks on everyone in the forest!
One winter day Fox trotted across the frozen lake, looking for food.
Suddenly she spotted a fisherman sitting by a hole in the ice.
"Yum!" Fox stared at the fisherman's long string of fish.
"Those fish look delicious. I wonder if . . ."
She crept closer.
When the fisherman looked away—
yank! Fox grabbed the string and
ran. Meanwhile Bear was looking for food
too. "I'd love to catch some fish," he
said. "But the lake is frozen
solid." Just then his eyes went
wide. Fox was racing by with a long string of
fish! Bear swished his tail in
excitement. "Fox! You caught so many
fish. I'm really hungry. Can you share some fish with
me?" "Ha!" Fox laughed
loudly. "This is my dinner, Bear. Catch your own
fish!" Bear frowned. "But the lake is frozen solid. How can I catch
fish?" "It's easy!" Fox hid her
grin. "Follow me, and I'll show you what to
do." Fox led Bear to the lake.
"First, make a hole in the ice.
Then, stick your tail in the hole.
It will hurt when the fish bite," she warned.
"But the longer you wait, the more fish you'll catch.
When you think you've caught enough fish, give a strong, hard pull."
"Got it!" Bear grinned.
Then he did just what Fox said.
Soon he felt a sharp pain in his tail.
"Wow!" Bear said. "I caught a fish already."
"Great!" Fox said.
"Remember—leave your tail in the water for as long as possible. Good luck!"
She ran off.
Bear sat on the ice all afternoon.
His tail hurt badly.
But he did his best to ignore the pain.
"After all, I'm catching lots of fish!" he thought.
Finally Bear was ready to eat.
He tried to pull his tail out of the ice. "Grr!"
His tail did not move.
He gave another hard pull.
But again nothing happened.
Then Bear pulled with all his might. Pop!
"Oh no!" Bear spun around.
Most of his tail was still stuck in the ice!
He roared with anger.
But it was too late.
Ever since this day, Bear has had a stumpy tail.
And Fox still laughs about her trick.

episodes.title: Why the Alligator's Back Is Rough

subtitle.text: Long ago Alligator stayed in the river during the daytime.
While the sun shone, he swam and rested in the cool water.
Only at night did Alligator climb out, letting moonlight wash over him.
One night Frog hopped closer and stared.
"Why, Alligator, you glow in the moonlight!"
Turtle lifted his head and nodded.
"The skin on your back is so smooth and golden!"
Alligator puffed up with pride. "Thank you, friends."
Their praise warmed him more than moonlight ever had.
The next day Alligator remembered their glowing words and admiring eyes.
"I felt so important," he thought.
"Like the king of the river! So why should I hide my beauty in darkness?
Everyone should see me clearly."
And so, when the sun next rose, Alligator crawled onto the riverbank.
"Good morning! Come see me—your golden king!"
"Alligator!" Frog hurried over.
"The sun is strong! It might burn your back."
Alligator laughed and flicked his tail.
"I'm much stronger than the sun!"
Along the river animals gathered, whispering and pointing.
"The skin on his back shines," Turtle said.
Otter nodded. "He looks so powerful."
"Like a river king!" Fish said.
Alligator grinned. "Move aside, Otter! You're blocking everyone's view."
He swung toward Beaver. "Bring me more food—now!"
High above, Vulture circled the riverbank.
He watched as animals scurried about, obeying Alligator's orders.
He listened as Alligator bragged loudly.
Finally Vulture flew down. "Pride grows heavy, Alligator.
It can weigh down even the strongest creature."
Alligator scoffed and waved his tail.
"You envy me, Vulture. Now fly away and leave me to my glory!"
He stretched across the hot riverbank and fell asleep.
When he woke, his skin stung and felt tight.
"Ouch!" he thought.
Still, he laughed loudly. "What a fine nap for a fine king!"
Each day Alligator returned to the sunny riverbank.
Each day his skin grew tighter and drier.
Soon the others began to hide from him.
"He's so bossy," Frog said.
Turtle nodded. "He brags too much."
One morning Frog stared. "Something's wrong."
"Alligator's skin is cracking!" Turtle cried.
Indeed, it was true.
Alligator's golden smoothness was gone.
Now ridges, bumps, and deep lines covered his back.
Vulture flew down.
"Nothing shines forever, Alligator. Especially too much pride."
Shame filled Alligator's heart. Slowly he slid back into the river.
"I ruined everything," he thought.
To this day, Alligator stays mostly hidden from others.
Only his eyes and nose appear above the water.
And forever, his back remains rough.

episodes.title: How the Old Woman Got Her Wish

subtitle.text: Once, an old woman lived with her son and his wife.
The woman was blind, and the family was very poor.
Yet each day the old woman prayed to a god.
Then, one morning, that god himself appeared before her.
"Old woman, you are thoughtful and kind.
You pray every day.
I would like to reward this goodness.
So I have decided to grant you a wish."
"What?" The old woman couldn't believe what she was hearing.
"But . . ." She bit her lip. "I don't know what to wish for."
"I understand," the god said.
"Talk to your son and his wife.
Surely they can help you decide what to choose.
I will return tomorrow."
The old woman hurried to her son.
"A god came to me. He said He will grant me one wish.
But what should I ask for?"
The son's face lit up.
"Our roof is leaking, and our clothes are thin.
Our rice pot is empty. Mother, you must ask for wealth!"
"Hmm." The old woman nodded slowly. "Maybe . . ."
Next she went to her son's wife.
"A god came to me. He said He will grant me one wish.
But what should I ask for?"
The younger woman's face lit up.
"You must ask for a baby—a beautiful grandson!"
"Hmm." The old woman nodded slowly, but she still felt unsure.
She went to visit a neighbor.
"A god says He will grant me one wish. But what should I ask for?"
The neighbor laughed.
"Why, you must ask Him for sight, of course. Just think!
You could see the blue sky and tall mountains again."
The old woman nodded.
But back at home, she paced across the floor.
"To make my son happy, I must ask for wealth," she thought.
"To make his wife happy, I must ask for a grandson.
To make myself happy, I must ask for sight.
But . . . I have just one wish. How can I make everyone happy?"
The next morning the god appeared.
"Well, old woman, it's time. What is your wish?"
The old woman took a deep breath.
She was ready.
"I wish to see my grandson drinking milk from a golden bowl."
"What?" The god laughed loudly.
"You clever old woman! You turned one wish into three!"
And so the wise old woman made everyone happy.
She prayed for the rest of her days, thankful for these gifts.
It was the night before Christmas.
And all through the house, everything was quiet—even my pet mouse!
But I couldn't sleep!
I lay awake in my bed.
Sweet thoughts of Christmas filled my head.
Suddenly I heard bells jingling from way up high.
I ran to the window and looked at the sky.
Something was flying in front of the moon.
"It's a sleigh!" I gasped.
"Santa Claus will be here soon!"
There were eight reindeer pulling Santa's sleigh.
I heard Santa calling each of their names.
"Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer and Vixen!
On, Comet! On, Cupid! On, Donner and Blitzen!"
Gently they landed on top of our roof.
I heard the sound of each reindeer hoof!
I sneaked from my room and went down the stairs.
I ducked down and hid behind a big chair.
Down through the chimney, Santa appeared.
He wore a red suit and had a fluffy, white beard.
He was carrying a sack of toys on his back.
He set it down and began to unpack.
Santa found the stockings and filled up each one.
But that's not the end—Santa's work wasn't done.
Next Santa took out some presents that were wrapped nicely.
Then he set them down under our Christmas tree.
Oops! That's when he saw me peeking around.
He gave me a friendly wink and didn't make a sound.
Now Santa's work was finally done.
He flew up the chimney, and then he was gone.
I opened the window to watch the sleigh fly.
The reindeer took off, and I waved good-bye.
"Ho, ho, ho!" Santa's jolly voice echoed as he flew out of sight.
"Merry Christmas to all, and to all a good night!"
Once upon a time, there lived a little Dutch boy.
No one knows if his story is true or what his name was.
Most people today call him Hans.
Hans lived in Haarlem, a city in the Netherlands.
The city was built on very low ground near the sea and had many canals.
Bricklayers had built walls called dikes to control the water in the canals.
The dikes kept the city from flooding.
One autumn day Hans' mother made some delicious cakes.
Hans thought of a blind man who lived on the other side of the city.
"Mother, may I take some cakes to Mr. van Beek?" he asked.
His mother smiled. "That's very kind of you."
She helped Hans get ready, putting on his scarf.
"Mr. van Beek loves to talk," his father said.
"Don't stay too late.
It looks like another storm is coming."
The day was cold and windy.
Hans skipped alongside the canals, full of water from the autumn rains.
A while later he arrived at Mr. van Beek's house.
Mr. van Beek was delighted to see his young friend.
"I can't stay long today," Hans said.
"But I'll come back soon to hear more stories!"
Hans left and was still far from home when the weather became stormy.
The wind burned his cheeks and whipped his scarf.
Suddenly Hans spotted something—a small hole in a dike.
"Uh-oh," he thought. "I need to find help."
He knew that a small hole could become a bigger hole.
If the hole became too big, the city might flood.
Hans looked around, but he didn't see anyone.
"Help!" he shouted, hoping someone would come running.
He kept shouting until his throat felt dry, but no one came.
He had to fix the problem on his own.
"Oh, what can I do?" he thought.
"I am only one little boy."
Finally he got an idea.
He wrapped his scarf around his hand.
Then he pushed his fist into the hole.
This stopped the water from coming through the dike.
The stormy night went on and on.
Hans shivered in the sharp wind.
"I must be strong," thought Hans.
"I must be brave like a grown-up."
Hans grew weary.
"I am so tired, but I must hold back the water."
Morning finally came and the storm passed.
An old man discovered Hans.
His hand was still in the dike.
He was shivering and exhausted from the cold.
But he had held back the sea all night.
"My goodness, child!" the man said.
"What are you doing here?"
"I'm holding back the water so the city won't flood," Hans said.
"Don't move! I'll be right back!"
The man hurried off to get help.
Soon he was back with Hans' parents.
"There you are, Hans!" his mother cried.
"We searched for you all night long!"
The city bricklayers came running to fix the dike.
Hans pulled out his fist, and they quickly sealed the hole.
"I did it," Hans thought.
Hans was bundled up in warm clothes.
He was very tired, but he smiled in the morning sun.
The storm had passed and his city was safe.
His mother and all the people of Haarlem were very proud of Hans.
The next day, a bright morning, the mayor awarded Hans a medal.
From that time on, Hans was known as the Little Hero of Haarlem.
Once upon a time, there was an old shoemaker.
Although he worked hard, he was very poor.
One cold winter night, he sat at his workbench.
He began cutting his last piece of leather.
There was only enough for one pair of shoes.
"Come to bed, dear," his wife said.
The shoemaker shook his head. "If
I don't sell these shoes, we'll have no money." "You
can finish them in the morning," the wife said. "Please,
get some rest." The
shoemaker sighed and put down his scissors. ***
In the middle of the night, two little elves climbed onto the workbench.
They wore thin rags for clothes and had no shoes.
They saw the cut leather and got to work.
And while they worked, they sang.
We are helpful little elves.
Helping others helps ourselves.
*** The next morning a beautiful pair of shoes sat on the
workbench. The shoemaker gasped. "Who made these
shoes?" "What a miracle!" the shoemaker's wife said.
That day a rich woman visited the shop.
She loved the shoes and paid more than the shoemaker had expected.
He was able to buy enough leather for two pairs of shoes.
That evening the shoemaker began cutting the leather.
He yawned as he cut.
"Dear, there's no need to work through the night," his wife said.
The shoemaker nodded. "I'll just finish cutting the leather."
When the shoemaker was finished, he left the leather on his workbench.
He yawned again and went to bed.
*** Once again the little elves visited the
shop. They happily got to work,
singing. We are helpful little elves.
Helping others helps ourselves.
*** The next morning two beautiful pairs of shoes sat finished on the
workbench. "It happened again!" the shoemaker
cried. "Someone must be trying to help us," his wife
said. The two pairs of shoes quickly
sold. Now there was enough money to buy leather for four pairs of
shoes. For several more days, the pattern
repeated. Eventually the shoemaker was no longer
poor. One evening, not long before Christmas, the shoemaker was cutting
leather. "Our fortunes have changed so quickly," his wife
said. "I wonder who has been helping
us." "Why don't we stay up tonight?" the shoemaker said.
"We can see who our kind helpers are."
"What a marvelous idea!" his wife said.
They hid and waited.
Before long the elves appeared on the workbench.
As the elves sang and worked, the shoemaker and his wife whispered to each other.
"Those poor creatures," she said.
"Their clothes are worn out."
"And they have no shoes," the shoemaker said.
"They helped us, so we should help them. I have an idea!"
*** On Christmas Eve the elves appeared
again. When they climbed onto the workbench, they
gasped. There was no leather cut for
shoes. Instead there were two sets of fine clothes and two fine pairs of shoes.
The elves quickly put everything on, singing.
We helped them. We did, indeed.
And they gave us the things we need.
The shoemaker and his wife watched the elves shuffle away.
The elves never visited the shop again.
But the shoemaker and his wife never forgot their kind helpers.
Once upon a time, there was a poor woodcutter.
He and his wife lived very simply.
The woodcutter often wished for more money and a better life.
But his wishes never came true.
One afternoon the woodcutter was searching for a tree to cut down.
All the trees looked too big or too small.
"I wish I could find a good tree," he said.
Like magic, he suddenly spotted the perfect one.
"My wish actually came true!"
The woodcutter raised his ax . . .
Suddenly a small fairy appeared.
"Stop! Please don't chop down my home."
The woodcutter frowned.
"I need wood to make money.
And all the other trees are too big or too small."
"How about this?" the fairy said.
"If you leave my tree alone, I will grant you three wishes."
"No, thanks," the woodcutter said.
"My wishes never come true."
"These wishes will come true," the fairy said.
"But if they don't, you may return and chop down my tree."
It was getting late, so the woodcutter agreed.
When he arrived home, he told his wife about the fairy and the wishes.
"Ridiculous!" she said.
"Tomorrow you will go back and chop down that dumb fairy's tree."
She set a bowl in front of him. "Here, have supper."
The woodcutter looked at his bowl and groaned.
"Plain broth again? I wish we had some sausages."
Poof! Two plump sausages appeared on the table.
The woodcutter was amazed. "My wish came true!"
"Indeed, it did!" His wife laughed.
"But you used up a wish on sausages. How silly!"
The woodcutter frowned. "It's not funny!
Why, I wish these sausages were stuck in your nose!"
Poof! Now it was the woodcutter's turn to laugh.
The sausages were stuck in his wife's nose!
"Stop laughing!" she snapped. "I wish—"
"No!" the woodcutter cried.
"Don't! There's only one wish left.
Let's try to get these sausages out of your nose first."
The woodcutter's wife pulled on a sausage, but it was stuck tightly.
"Let me try." The woodcutter slowly pulled on a sausage.
"Ow! Stop! It hurts!"
The woodcutter let go.
"Let's put some grease on the sausages.
Then they'll slide out easily."
He spread some butter on the sausages.
He tried to pull again.
"Ouch!" his wife cried. "It's not working."
"What should we do?" the woodcutter asked.
"We still have one wish left," his wife said.
"And I can't live with sausages in my nose."
"You're right. I wish . . ." The woodcutter took a deep breath.
"The sausages were out of my wife's nose!"
Poof! The sausages lay on the table again.
The woodcutter and his wife looked at them sadly.
"We wasted the wishes," the woodcutter said.
"At least the sausages are out of my nose," his wife said.
Then she smiled. "And you did wish for sausages with supper!"
She began to laugh again.
"I'm not eating those! They were in your nose."
The woodcutter laughed too.
They were no better off than they had been before.
But their three ridiculous wishes sure made them laugh.
Long ago a boy named Jack lived with his mother.
They were very poor.
Jack's mother worked hard, but Jack was lazy.
He spent his days playing and singing silly songs.
Sometimes he stared at a castle in the distance.
"I wonder who lives there," he thought.
As he grew older, his mother grew impatient.
"You need to find work," she said.
"I will do my best, Mother!" Jack promised.
Jack was not very bright, but he was kind.
He soon found work at a mill.
He worked hard, and the miller paid him a silver coin.
On his way home, Jack crossed a stream, and—
splash! He dropped the
coin. When Jack returned home, his mother
moaned. "Oh, you silly boy! You must put your pay in your
pocket." "I will do that," Jack
said. Next Jack found work at a
bakery. The baker paid him with a loaf of
bread. Jack stuffed the bread into his
pocket. "Mother! I put my pay in my
pocket!" Jack pulled out the
bread. Crumbs spilled
everywhere. "Oh, you silly boy! You must carry your pay on your
head!" Next Jack worked on a
farm. His pay was a large jar of
milk. "I must carry this jar on my head," Jack thought.
Jack carefully put the jar on his head.
But on his way home, it fell off. Crash!
Mother sighed. "Oh, you silly boy!
You must carry your pay on your shoulders."
Next Jack worked at the market.
"You work hard, Jack," his boss said.
"I will pay you with this donkey."
"I must put my pay on my shoulders," Jack thought.
Jack put the donkey on his shoulders.
As he walked, he wobbled this way and that way.
"This donkey is very heavy!" Jack thought.
"I'll sing a silly song.
That will make the trip easier."
"Doodle-dee-doo! Doodle-dee-doo!"
"Hee-haw!" The donkey seemed to sing along.
Jack tried hard not to drop the donkey.
So he didn't see the king and the princess pass by.
The princess saw Jack zigzagging.
She heard the funny song and burst into laughter.
The king's eyes lit up.
The princess stopped smiling after her mother died.
Now she couldn't stop laughing.
"You!" the king yelled to Jack. "Come and meet the princess!"
Soon Jack was a regular visitor at the castle.
He and the princess laughed and sang.
"Doodle-dee-doo! Doodle-dee-doo!"
Later, of course, they got married, and lived very happily ever after.
Once upon a time, there was a girl named Goldilocks.
Goldilocks loved walking in the woods.
But sometimes she was not kind to the animals who lived there.
She chased the birds and mice.
She splashed the turtles and fish.
She hid the squirrels' acorns.
One day Goldilocks was in the woods when she spotted a house.
Goldilocks did not know that the house belonged to three bears.
She opened the door and went inside.
On the table were three bowls of porridge.
"I'm hungry," Goldilocks thought.
She tasted the porridge in the biggest bowl. "Too hot!" Next
she tried the porridge in the medium bowl. "Too cold!" Then
she tasted the porridge in the littlest bowl. "Just right!" After
eating, Goldilocks went into the living room. "I'll
take a rest," she thought. She
sat in the biggest chair. "This
chair is too hard!" She
tried the next chair. "Too soft!" The
smallest chair looked just right. But
when Goldilocks sat in it— crash!
The chair broke!
Goldilocks sighed. "I'll just look for a bed," she thought.
Upstairs, Goldilocks found three beds.
The first one was too high.
The second one was too low.
The third one was . . .
"Just right!" Goldilocks said happily.
She climbed into the bed and pulled up the covers.
Soon she was fast asleep.
*** The three bears were on their way home from the
stream. "That was a nice morning walk," Mama Bear
said. "Now it's time for
breakfast." Papa Bear rubbed his belly. "I'm
hungry." "Me too," Baby Bear said. "I love
porridge." But when they arrived home, Mama
gasped. "Someone tasted my
porridge!" Papa growled. "Someone tasted my porridge
too!" "Well, someone tasted my porridge—and ate it all up!" Baby
said. Mama pointed to their chairs. "Someone sat in our chairs!"
"Look!" Baby sniffed. "My chair is broken!"
The three bears hurried upstairs.
"Somebody was sleeping in my bed!" Papa said.
"Somebody was sleeping in my bed!" Mama said.
"Somebody is sleeping in my bed!" Baby cried. "Ahh!"
Baby Bear's scream woke up Goldilocks.
"Oh no!" she cried. "Bears!"
Goldilocks hopped out of bed and raced downstairs.
She ran through the woods as fast as she could.
At last she was home.
After that, Goldilocks still loved walking in the woods.
But now she was always kind to the animals!
One day a husband and wife decided to make a gingerbread cookie.
They cut the dough and baked it.
When it was ready, they decorated its face with candy.
"There!" The woman smiled. "He almost looks real."
Her husband nodded. "He sure does."
To their surprise, the cookie suddenly jumped up.
He ran out the door.
The couple ran after him. "Come back!"
The cookie just laughed and ran faster.
"Run, run, as fast as you can!
You can't catch me. I'm the gingerbread man."
Soon the cookie ran past a dog.
The dog barked. "Mmm! I'm going to eat you!"
The cookie laughed.
"Run, run as fast as you can!
You can't catch me. I'm the gingerbread man."
The dog ran after the cookie, but the cookie ran faster.
Soon the cookie ran past a child.
"Mmm!" the child said. "I'm going to eat you!"
The cookie laughed.
"Run, run as fast as you can!
You can't catch me. I'm the gingerbread man."
The child ran after the cookie, but the cookie ran faster.
Soon the cookie ran past a cow.
The cow mooed. "Mmm! I'm going to eat you!"
The cookie laughed.
"Run, run, as fast as you can!
You can't catch me. I'm the gingerbread man."
The cookie ran until he reached a river.
"Uh-oh!" he said. "I can't swim!"
"Do you want to cross the river?" someone asked.
The cookie spun around. A fox stood nearby.
"Oh yes!" the gingerbread man said.
"Can you help me?"
"Sure," the fox said.
"Jump on my tail. I'll take you to the other side."
"Great!" The cookie jumped onto the fox's tail.
The fox started across the river.
"Hmm," she said.
"The water is getting deep.
Why don't you climb onto my back?"
The fox kept swimming.
"The water is getting even deeper.
Why don't you climb onto my nose?"
"Okay," the cookie said. "Thanks for keeping me so safe."
"No problem," the fox said.
Then . . . she gobbled up the cookie in one bite! Snap!
At last everyone reached the river.
"The gingerbread man is gone!" the child said sadly.
The husband nodded.
But the wife smiled.
"Come home with us. We'll make another gingerbread man!"
So everyone went home with the husband and wife.
Together they made another gingerbread man.
And this one was delicious!
Farmer planted turnip seeds.
He watered them every day.
One turnip grew and grew and grew.
Finally the enormous turnip was ready to eat.
Farmer pulled.
But it didn't move.
"Wife!" called Farmer.
"Help me pull this turnip!"
His wife pulled too.
But the turnip didn't move.
A boy with a dog came over.
"My dog and I can help," he said.
They all pulled.
But the turnip still didn’t move.
Then a cat came along.
Everyone pulled together.
The turnip moved . . . a little.
Finally Farmer sighed.
"This turnip is too big. I give up."
"I can help!" said a mouse.
Everyone laughed.
"This is an enormous turnip!" said Farmer.
"You're just a little mouse!"
But Farmer let Mouse help.
"Ready?" said Farmer.
"Ready!" said everyone.
Together they pulled.
Suddenly . . . Pop!
Out came the turnip!
"We did it!" cried Mouse.
"We all worked together," said Farmer.
"Whew! Next year I'll plant pumpkins!"
In the spring, Little Red Hen was busy.
She was planning for the winter.
She decided to plant some wheat.
"Cluck, cluck. Who will help me plant this wheat?" she asked.
"Baa, baa. Not I. I have to rest," said the goat.
"Oink, oink. Not I. I must take a nap," said the pig.
"Okay, I will plant the wheat by myself," said Little Red Hen.
When the summer came, the wheat began to grow.
The weeds grew too.
"Cluck, cluck. Who will help me pluck the weeds?" asked Little Red Hen.
"Baa, baa. Not I. It is too hot outside," said the goat.
"Oink, oink. Not I. I have to cool off in the mud," said the pig.
"Okay, I will weed the wheat all by myself," said Little Red Hen.
When the fall came, the wheat was ripe.
"Cluck, cluck. Who will help me harvest the wheat?" she asked.
"Baa, baa. Not I. I am going to a party," said the goat.
"Oink, oink. Not I. I am eating lunch," said the pig.
"Okay, I will harvest the wheat all by myself," said Little Red Hen.
She harvested the wheat.
Then she took it to the mill and ground it into flour.
In the winter, there was very little to eat.
But Little Red Hen had flour to make bread.
"Cluck, cluck. Who will help me bake the bread?" she asked.
"Baa, baa. Not I. I am too tired," said the goat.
"Oink, oink. Not I. I want to sleep some more," said the pig.
"Okay, I will bake the bread by myself," she said.
When the bread was done, Little Red Hen opened the oven.
The bread smelled delicious!
"Cluck, cluck! Who wants my bread now?" she asked.
"Baa, baa! Me, me! It smells really good!" said the goat.
"Oink, oink! Me too! It looks delicious!" said the pig.
"No, you won't.
Whenever I needed help, you did not help me.
I will eat it all by myself," answered Little Red Hen.
So the goat and the pig stayed hungry.
Little Red Hen ate the whole loaf of bread all by herself.
Henny Penny was a chicken.
She was a hungry chicken.
One day, she was looking for food on the ground.
Suddenly, a nut fell off of a tree.
The nut hit Henny Penny on the head.
"Oh my! The sky is falling!
I must tell the king!" Henny Penny said.
She ran by the barn.
Cocky Locky said, "Cock-a-doodle-doo!
Henny Penny, where are you going?"
Henny Penny replied, "The sky is falling!
I must tell the king!
Why don't you come too?"
"I will!" Cocky Locky said.
They ran by the lake.
Ducky Lucky said, "Quack, quack, Henny Penny and Cocky Locky!
Where are you going?"
They replied, "The sky is falling!
We must tell the king!
Why don't you come too?"
"I will!" Ducky Lucky said.
They ran by the river.
Goosey Loosey said, "Honk, honk, Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, and Ducky Lucky!
Where are you going?"
They replied, "The sky is falling!
We must tell the king!
Why don't you come too?"
"I will!" Goosey Loosey said.
They ran into the forest.
Turkey Lurkey said, "Gobble, gobble, gobble, Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Lucky, and Goosey Loosey!
Where are you going?"
They replied, "The sky is falling!
We must tell the king!
Why don't you come too?"
"I will!" Turkey Lurkey said.
They ran by a cave.
Foxy Loxy saw Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Lucky, Goosey Loosey, and Turkey Lurkey.
"I will invite them into my cave.
Then, I can eat them!" said Foxy Loxy.
"Ah, Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Lucky, Goosey Loosey, and Turkey Lurkey!
Where are you going?"
They replied, "The sky is falling!
We must tell the king!
Why don't you come too?"
"I will! But first, rest in my cave," said Foxy Loxy.
Suddenly, a nut fell off of a tree.
The nut hit Foxy Loxy on the head.
"Oh my! The sky is falling!
We must tell the king!
You must come too!" she cried.
But Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Lucky, Goosey Loosey, and Turkey Lurkey said, "The sky is not falling.
A nut fell on your head!
Let's all go home."
But Foxy Loxy kept saying, "The sky is falling!
The sky is falling!"
Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Lucky, Goosey Loosey, and Turkey Lurkey all laughed.
Foxy Loxy shouted again, "The sky is falling!"
Then she ran away to tell the king.
Narrator: Many years ago, England was going through hard times.
Some villages were very poor. But
everyone still needed to eat and laugh. This
is a story about how strangers become friends. Morris: I
say, Stanley, this looks like a good spot. Stanley: Right-o,
Morris. We’ll stop here for the evening. Morris:
Shall we start making the soup? Stanley:
A fine idea. I’ll
get the water and a stone. Narrator:
Morris and Stanley were on their way to London.
They were traveling on foot. Along
the way Morris and Stanley stopped at villages. Each time,
they made stone soup. Stanley: Morris, old
pal, here’s the water. Morris: Smells delicious.
Stanley: And
here’s a stone. Morris: That’s
a fine one, Stanley. Our soup
will be very tasty tonight. Narrator: Just
then Mrs. Tweedy from the village and her son Wilbert walked by. They
were returning from the market. Morris: Good
day, madam. Mrs. Tweedy:
Good day, gentlemen. Stanley: Would
you care to join us for some soup? Wilbert: Oh,
yes please! Mrs. Tweedy:
Wilbert! We must get home and prepare supper. Morris:
Wilbert? Is that your name? Wilbert:
Yes, sir, it is. Morris:
Why, that boy with the three-legged cat was named Wilbert too. Wilbert:
Three-legged cat?
What happened to its other leg?
Morris: Well, it was born with four legs, of course, but then . . .
Narrator: Morris and Stanley told the story of the boy with the three-legged
cat. Even Wilbert’s mother listened.
Just then Mr. Podger from the village walked by. He
was carrying a loaf of bread. Morris: .
. . And that’s the story. Wilbert:
Is it true? Mr.
Podger: Is what true? What’s
going on here? Mrs.
Tweedy: Oh, Mr. Podger, please come and meet Morris and Stanley. Narrator:
Everyone said hello to each other.
Stanley: Morris, is it just me or does Mr. Podger remind you of someone?
Morris: Hmm, yes. He reminds me of Otis and Oliver, the twin barbers!
Stanley: Exactly what I was
thinking. Mr. Podger: Twin barbers?
Where? Stanley: In Windermere. They’re quite the barbers, Otis and Oliver. You see . .
. Narrator: Mr. Podger sat down and listened to the story of the
twin barbers. A few minutes later, Miss Mabel from the village walked
by. She was carrying a bag of potatoes.
Miss Mabel: Good day, all.
May I ask what you’re doing
here? Mr. Podger: Miss Mabel! Come and meet Morris and
Stanley. Morris: I say, Miss Mabel, what a splendid
coat. Miss Mabel: Why, thank
you. Stanley: It looks like the one worn by Queen Francesca
of Spain. Morris: Indeed! We met her
in Chester. Miss Mabel: A coat like mine on
a queen? Do
tell all! Narrator: So Morris and Stanley told the story of
the Spanish queen. Everyone laughed. They had a great time talking with
the strangers. Before long, it was getting
dark. Mrs. Tweedy: Thank you for a
lovely time. Mr. Podger: I haven’t laughed so much
in ages. Miss Mabel: Oh, I hope your soup is
not ruined. Wilbert: Why is there a stone in
the soup? Morris: Because
it’s stone soup. Mrs. Tweedy: That doesn’t
sound very tasty. Stanley: It’s
actually quite good. Morris: Last night it
tasted of turnips. Stanley: And the night before, it
tasted of peas. Narrator: Now, the villagers did not think stone
soup could be tasty. They looked at each
other and wondered. Morris: Oh yes, this
is very tasty. What do
you think, Stanley? Stanley: Delicious! But I think it needs just
a little extra something. Mrs. Tweedy: I have some
carrots and onions here. Let’s put them in
the soup. Miss Mabel: I have some potatoes.
In they go! Mr. Podger: And I’ve
got fresh bread. Just the thing to
have with soup. Narrator: Stanley and Morris took turns
stirring the pot. Soon the stone soup turned into a
hearty vegetable soup. Stanley: The best I’ve ever
tasted! Help yourselves! Morris: Delicious! Which reminds me of another story
. . . Narrator: So Morris told them
another funny story. Everyone
ate and laughed. It was
a wonderful evening. Mr. Podger: You must come and stay the night
at my house. Morris and Stanley: Oh,
thank you, sir! Narrator: Morris and Stanley
left the next morning. But the villagers never forgot
the two men. They often talked about how Morris and Stanley made
them laugh. And everyone remembered their wonderfully delicious stone
soup. The people of this town had been
strangers. But now they were friends. The end.
Narrator: Once upon a time, there lived three little pigs.
Their names were Curly, Chunky, and Pinky. One
day they decided to see the world. Mama:
Bye-bye, boys. Take care. Curly,
Chunky, and Pinky: Bye, Mama! Pinky:
Well, I’m going this direction. Chunky:
I’m going that way. Curly:
I think I’ll head over there. Narrator:
The three pigs went in different directions. Curly
met a goat selling straw. Curly: I’ll
build a house of straw. Narrator: So
he bought some straw and built his house. Curly:
There, what a cozy home! Narrator:
Curly relaxed in his new home. But
there was one problem . . . Willis:
Knock-knock! Oh, yoo-hoo! Curly:
Who’s there? Willis:
A friend, Willis the Wolf. Now
let me in. Narrator:
Mama Pig taught her sons never to open the door to strangers, especially strangers with big teeth!
Curly: No, no! Not by the hair on my chinny-chin-chin.
Willis: Let me in!
Or I'll huff and I'll puff and I'll blow your house down.
Curly: No! You can't come in, you big bully!
Willis: I’m going to
huff! I’m going to
puff! And I’m going to blo-o-o-o-w-w-w your house down!
Narrator: It wasn’t that hard.
Straw houses fall easily.
Willis: Now, little pig.
I’m going to eat you up!
Curly: Help!
Narrator: Meanwhile, Chunky met a beaver selling sticks.
Chunky: I’ll build a house of sticks.
Narrator: So he bought some sticks and built his
house. Chunky: There, what a pleasant
home! Narrator: Chunky looked at his new house with
pride. But there was one problem . . .
Curly: Chunky, h-h-help!
Chunky: Eek! It’s a wolf!
Hurry inside. Lock the door.
Willis: Knock-knock! Let me in!
Chunky: No! Not by the hair on my
chinny-chin-chin. Willis: Let me
in! Or I'll huff and I'll puff and I'll blow your house
down. Chunky: You can't come
in! Willis: I’m going to
huff! I’m going to
puff! And I’m going to blo-o-o-o-w-w-w your house down!
Narrator: It wasn’t that hard.
Stick houses fall
easily. Willis: Now I’m going to eat you
up! Curly and Chunky:
Help! Narrator: Meanwhile, Pinky met a horse selling
bricks. Pinky: I’ll build my house with
bricks. Narrator: So he bought some bricks and started his
house. Pinky: This will be a strong
home. Narrator: Pinky took his time to build a
brick house. Pinky: My house is
almost finished. I'll put one more brick on
the chimney. Narrator: But there was one problem .
. . Curly and Chunky:
Pinky, h-h-help! Chunky: A wolf is
chasing us! Curly: Get inside quick and lock
the door! Willis: Well what do
we have here? That pig is trapped
on the roof. There’s no place for him
to run. Hello,
little pig! Pinky: It’s that bully,
the wolf. What will I do?
I know! Narrator: Pinky climbed into his chimney and
slid down. In the house, Curly and Chunky were
scared. Curly: The wolf is
chasing us! Chunky: He’s going to eat
us up! Pinky: I have
an idea! Fill that pot
with water. Narrator: Pinky built a
hot fire. Then the three little pigs put the pot on the
fire. Willis: Knock-knock! Let me
in! Pinky: No! Not by the hair on my
chinny-chin-chin! Willis: I blew down a
straw house. I blew down a
stick house. I’ll huff and I’ll puff and I’ll blow your house down
too! Pinky: Go ahead and
try! Willis: I’m going to
huff! I’m going to
puff! And I’m going to blo-o-o-o-w-w-w your house down!
Pinky: I’m waiting!
Willis: I said, I’m going to blo-o-o-o-w-w-w your house
down! Narrator: Brick houses don’t fall so
easily. Willis: It doesn’t
matter. I can be as clever as the
pig! Curly: Oh no, he's climbing up the
house. Chunky: He’s climbing onto the
roof! Pinky: Let’s see. The water is boiling nice and
hot. Willis: I’ll slide down the chimney just like
that pig! Narrator: Willis licked his lips and hopped down
the chimney. But there was just one problem . .
. When Willis fell in, Pinky covered the pot.
Willis: Ahh! Oww! Let me out!
Pinky: I’ll let you out if you promise to leave us
alone. Willis: I
promise! Narrator: Willis left town and never came
back. Pinky: We won’t see him
again! Curly: Well, it’s time to build another
house. Chunky: Let’s get
started! Narrator: Pinky helped his
brothers. When Mama Pig came, they all had new, strong brick homes.
Mama: What beautiful homes,
boys! I'm glad you built your houses of
brick. You never know what might happen!
Narrator: And the three little pigs smiled. The end.
Once upon a time, there were two good brothers who lived in the country.
Both brothers were rice farmers.
The older brother was married and he lived with his family.
The younger brother was unmarried and lived with their mother.
The brothers worked hard in the rice fields.
They began early in the morning and finished late at night.
Summer ended and it became fall─time to harvest the rice.
It was a good year and both brothers harvested a lot of rice.
The older brother looked at his rice and was happy.
Then he thought, "My younger brother looks after our mother.
Maybe he needs more rice."
That night, the older brother waited until everyone had gone to sleep.
He took three bundles of rice and secretly carried them to his brother's field.
On that same night, the younger brother thought,
"My older brother is married and has a family.
Maybe he needs some extra rice."
He carried three bundles of rice to his older brother's field.
The next morning, both brothers awakened early.
When they came to the fields, they checked on their rice.
"What?" they both thought.
"Yesterday I had twenty bundles of rice.
Last night I took some bundles to my brother's, but today I still have twenty bundles of rice.
Was it all a dream?"
During the day, the brothers worked hard in the fields.
That night, the older brother took some more bundles of rice to his younger brother's field.
He thought, "My younger brother must find a wife.
He should have lots of rice."
That night, the younger brother thought,
"My older brother's wife is having a baby soon.
He should have more rice."
He carried some bundles of rice to his older brother's field and left them there.
The next day, the older brother was surprised again.
He still had twenty bundles of rice!
The younger brother was also surprised.
He still had twenty bundles of rice.
How could this be?
That night, both brothers waited until it was dark.
They each put four bundles of rice on their shoulders and walked toward the fields.
The older brother saw a man in the distance.
"How strange! Who is walking so late?"
The younger brother also saw a man in the distance.
"That's funny," he thought.
"The man is carrying something.
It's very late."
Both brothers kept walking toward the fields and they met.
"It was you!" the older brother and the younger brother shouted.
The two brothers hugged each other.
"What a wonderful brother I have," they each thought.

episodes.title: The Old Man and His Cyst

subtitle.text: There once lived an old man who had a cyst on his cheek.
It was a rather big, ugly cyst and very hard to hide.
"Ooh! I wish you were gone!" the man shouted at his cyst.
The old man took medicines and applied creams.
He even tried removing it by force.
Whatever he did was useless because the cyst continued to grow bigger each day.
Despite the ugly cyst, the old man had a good heart.
He shared what he had with others.
"I have more than enough!" he often said.
While walking home one day, the sky suddenly turned dark.
A terrible thunderstorm began, so the man ran for shelter.
He found a hollow tree and hid inside it until the storm passed.
When the rain finally stopped, the man stepped out of the tree.
Suddenly he heard strange sounds of laughter and singing.
"What in the world?" he wondered.
The old man gasped at the sight.
Just behind the tree, a group of goblins had gathered.
They appeared to be having a party—dancing, singing, and drinking.
As the old man watched, he soon began to enjoy himself too.
One of the goblins was a terrible dancer.
The goblin leader could not stand to watch him anymore.
"Stop! You’re making me dizzy!
Can anyone teach this poor goblin to dance?" he begged.
"Oh, I can!"
The old man stepped into their view.
"I used to be a dancer. See?" the old man said cheerfully.
He showed the goblins his dancing skills.
Well, there was no doubt, the old man knew how to move.
All the goblins, including the leader, were impressed.
"You must come back tomorrow night and teach us more steps!" said the leader.
"I can teach you the tango!" the old man replied eagerly.
"As a sign of promise, give me something that belongs to you," said the leader.
He then removed the cyst from the man’s face.
It was gone!
The big, ugly cyst was finally gone.
The old man ran home and told his wife the strange story.
"Your skin is smooth as a baby’s," his wife remarked.
"Just look at me!
My cyst is gone forever!"
The man began to dance.
Next door lived the greedy landlord of the house.
His favorite pastime was counting his money and gold.
Unfortunately for him, he had a big, ugly cyst too, but on his left cheek.
"I’m here to collect the rent," he told the old man.
"I’m sorry, but I promise to pay it by tomorrow," the old man begged.
"What happened to your cyst?" the landlord pointed.
The old man told him about the goblins.
"Then in exchange for your rent, I shall go see these goblins tonight," the greedy man replied.
The old man had no choice but to allow the landlord to go instead of him.
The landlord did exactly as the old man did.
He hid in the hollow tree and waited until it got dark.
Soon he heard dancing and singing, just as the old man had said.
The leader of the goblins looked around.
"I hope the old man keeps his promise," he said.
At that moment the greedy landlord jumped out, spreading his fans.
Pretending to be the old man, he began dancing.
But unfortunately he was an awful dancer!
"What happened to the tango?" asked one goblin.
"Forget the tango.
Do this!" the old man shouted back.
He jumped up and down like a chicken.
Finally the leader could stand it no more.
"Stop it! We were wrong!
You are a horrible dancer," yelled the leader.
"Here, I give you back what I took!"
The leader threw the cyst onto the right cheek.
The landlord was greedy and had tricked the goblins.
So he was left with a cyst on each cheek.

episodes.title: The Man, the Snake, and the Fox

subtitle.text: One fine morning, a man was taking a walk.
"Help me," a voice cried out.
A snake was trapped under a pile of rocks.
"Please help me.
I'm stuck!" begged the snake.
The man shook his head.
"No, because you will eat me!"
"Oh no! I would never eat you!" promised the snake.
The man believed the snake.
So, he helped the snake from under the rocks.
"Ah, now I feel hungry," said the snake.
"You promised not to eat me," said the man.
"Yes, but my stomach didn't," the sly snake hissed.
The man was very afraid.
"Wait! Let's ask the other animals what to do," the man said.
First, the man and the snake met a dog.
They told him the story and asked, "What should we do?"
"The dog replied, "I used to hunt rabbits and birds for my master.
But he never gave me good food to eat.
Now I'm old," continued the dog, "and my master wants to kill me."
He looked at the man angrily.
"So I think the snake should eat you!"
Next, they met a horse.
They told him the story and asked, "What should we do?"
The horse replied, "I used to carry things for my master.
Now that I'm old, my master wants to kill me!"
He looked at the man angrily.
"So I think the snake should eat you!"
"See? Two animals say I should eat you," the snake said happily.
"Wait! Let's ask one more animal," begged the man.
"Please, Fox, we have a question to ask."
They told him the story.
"Where did you find the snake?" the fox asked.
The man pointed to the rocks.
"What were you doing?" the fox asked the snake.
"I was here, asking the man for help."
The snake showed them how he got stuck.
"Is that the way you were?" asked the fox.
"Yes, yes! Now get me out."
The snake tried to lift the rocks, but couldn't.
"Then that is how you shall stay," the fox smiled slyly.
Once upon a time, there lived a beautiful girl.
Jingnyeo was the daughter of the king of heaven.
Her father loved her very much.
Jingnyeo was beautiful and kindhearted.
She was also an excellent weaver.
The king decided it was time for Jingnyeo to get married.
A search began to find her a husband, but it was not easy.
After many days, the king was about to give up.
Finally one day, the king found the perfect husband for Jingnyeo.
"Yes, that's him!
He will marry my daughter!" shouted the excited king.
And so, Kyunwoo the cattle farmer and Jingnyeo were married.
Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo loved each other very much.
They spent every day together.
"Kyunwoo! Mind your cows!" the angry king yelled.
"Oh, I beg your mercy, Your Highness," giggled Kyunwoo.
Jingnyeo did not have time for her weaving.
Kyunwoo did not have time for his cows.
They only had time for each other.
The king was very angry at Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo.
"Since you got married, you have become lazy!" scolded the king.
"Look at your cows!
Look at your weaving frame!
For this, you, Kyunwoo, will be sent to the east!
And you, Jingnyeo, will be sent to the west!"
Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo began crying before the king.
"On the seventh day of July, you shall meet," the king continued.
"But the Milky Way will separate you forever!"
So after one year, on the seventh day of July, they saw each other again.
It was not a happy meeting.
Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo longed to be together.
But the Milky Way still lay between them.
Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo were not the only ones who were unhappy.
"It must be the seventh day of July again!" shouted the animals and the birds.
Every year, Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo's tears fell to the earth.
Their many tears caused floods.
The creatures of the earth held a meeting.
"It is because Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo are apart!" complained the crow.
"Their tears cause the floods!" sniffed the deer.
"They must meet or we will all die from their tears!" said the rabbit.
"But how? The Milky Way stands between them!" cried the deer.
All the creatures thought and thought what to do.
Finally, they came up with a brilliant plan.
All the crows on the earth gathered together.
They flew up to the sky, higher and higher.
Then one by one, the birds lay down and formed a bridge.
It was the day for Kyunwoo and Jingnyeo to meet again.
"What is this? It is a bridge for me to cross!"
Kyunwoo exclaimed when he saw what the crows had done.
"Can this be true?
Is that my beloved husband?" Jingnyeo shouted.
At last, Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo were together once again.
Thanks to the birds and the bridge they made, Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo could meet every year.
On a clear night, you can still see Jingnyeo and Kyunwoo in the stars.
Jingnyeo as the harp and Kyunwoo as the eagle are separated by the Milky Way.
It no longer floods on the seventh day of July.
But it may rain a little—not from tears of sorrow, but from tears of joy.
Once upon a time, there lived a young man named Narcissus.
He was handsome.
In fact, he was the most beautiful man in the world.
Narcissus did not know how handsome he was.
But his mother did.
She worried about him all the time.
"What are you holding in your hand, Mother?"
Narcissus pointed at the mirror.
"It is nothing," she answered.
"Well, good night then," he shrugged.
Narcissus’ mother always said to him.
"If you do not look at yourself, you will live a long life."
But Narcissus wanted to fall in love.
"How can I fall in love if I don’t know what I look like?" he said to himself.
Every day Narcissus took long walks in the woods.
"I wish I could fall in love," Narcissus said to himself.
Narcissus did not know that many women already loved him.
One day Narcissus walked to the deepest part of the woods.
"Oh, what’s that?" he said, as he noticed a small pond.
"I’ve never seen a pond here before."
"Oh! Oh!" Narcissus suddenly cried out.
For inside the pond was the most beautiful person he had ever seen!
"Where have you been all my life?" he whispered lovingly.
Narcissus, of course, was looking at his own reflection in the water.
"Can there be anyone more beautiful than you?" he asked his reflection.
"At last I have finally found my true love."
It was almost dark and Narcissus had not returned home.
"He has been gone too long!" his mother worried.
"I wonder if something has happened to him."
"Eating, sleeping? What good is it to me?" Narcissus spoke gently.
"If I can’t be with you, what reason is there to live?"
That day Narcissus did not return home.
In fact, for many, many days, Narcissus did not eat or sleep.
He was deeply in love—with himself!
Finally Narcissus died looking at himself in the pond.
After he died, Narcissus’ body turned into a beautiful flower.
The flower’s head bends over, like Narcissus peering into the water.
It looks at the loveliest sight in the whole world.
For Narcissus it was beauty to die for.
Two sisters were watching the stars one night.
"Which is your favorite?" asked the younger sister.
"I like Bright Star.
It is the prettiest, and one day I will marry that star," replied the older sister.
The two sisters laughed, and then went inside to bed.
The next morning the two sisters were walking through the woods.
The older sister saw a white cat caught in a tree.
The beautiful cat looked very scared, and so the older sister decided to climb the tree and rescue it.
As the older sister climbed the tree, the cat also climbed higher.
In fact, as the cat climbed higher, the tree grew taller.
So, the older sister kept climbing and climbing, trying to help the cat.
Soon they were very high above the forest.
But the cat kept climbing.
Then, to the girl’s surprise, she had reached the stars.
She stepped off the tree and into the world of the stars.
The cat was not a cat at all.
He was a very handsome star man.
"What am I doing here?" asked the girl.
"Last night you said that you wanted to marry me," replied the man.
"So, I brought you here to the star world.
You can live in this beautiful land with me."
The star people were very kind, and the star man was a wonderful husband.
Soon the girl was very happy in the beautiful star world.
In fact, soon the girl turned into a star herself.
One day, the star man said to his new wife,
"You may go anywhere you like.
But please do not pick any white turnips.
King Star has made it a rule."
One day, when the girl was in the garden, she saw the white turnips.
She became very curious, and she decided to pick just one.
It was very difficult to pick the turnip.
She had to pull and pull.
When she finally pulled the turnip, there was a large hole.
The girl peeked through the hole.
Down below she could see her younger sister watching the stars.
Her younger sister looked very sad and lonely.
This made the older sister sad too because she missed her younger sister a lot.
The older sister created a plan.
She would make a rope so that she could climb up and down between the stars and the earth.
When the long rope was finished, she began to climb down.
But the rope was not nearly long enough.
She tried to climb back up, but she was not strong enough.
Soon, she lost her grip and fell to the earth.
The younger sister watched the stars every night.
One night she saw a beautiful falling star.
As she watched the bright star fall, she remembered her older sister.
She pictured her sister’s face and missed her even more.
But she knew that she would never see her older sister again.
Long, long ago, a mole couple’s daughter, Mollie, was ready to marry.
In the mole village, Moler was the best available bridegroom.
However, Father Mole and Mother Mole were not satisfied with him.
"Isn't there a better bridegroom?" asked Mollie's mother.
"Our Mollie must marry the greatest bridegroom," said her father.
Father Mole and Mother Mole discussed the matter.
"Who do you think is the greatest of all?" Father wondered aloud.
"I think the sun is the greatest," Mother answered.
Father Mole went to the sun.
"Gosh! It's so hot!
Sun, are you the greatest of all?" he asked.
"No, I'm not.
When the cloud comes and covers me, I can't even show my face.
The cloud is the greatest," the sun replied.
"Oh, I see. Thank you."
Father Mole went to see the cloud.
"Oh my, it's so dark!
Cloud, are you the greatest of all?" he asked.
"No, I'm not.
When the wind comes, I'm blown away in seconds.
The wind is the greatest," replied the cloud.
"Oh, I see. Thank you."
Father Mole went to see the wind.
"Oh my, I'm about to be blown away!
Wind, you are the greatest of all, right?" he asked hopefully.
"No, I'm not.
There is someone who doesn't blow away even when I blow my hardest," said the wind.
"Is that true?" asked Father Mole.
"Mr. Mole, if you are looking for the greatest, go to the Buddha statue," advised the wind.
Though Father Mole was tired, he went to see the Buddha statue.
"Finally I've found it.
Buddha statue, you are the greatest in the world, right?" Father Mole asked.
"No, I'm not.
If a mole dug a hole under my feet, I could not stand for even a minute," the Buddha statue answered.
"Do you think the mole is the best bridegroom in the world?" asked Father Mole.
"Definitely! Ha-ha-ha!" the Buddha statue answered with laughter.
Father Mole then went back to the mole village.
"Honey! I've found someone who is the greatest," he declared to his wife.
"Oh really!" Mother replied.
Father Mole explained.
"The sun said, 'The cloud is the greatest.'
The cloud said, 'The wind is the greatest.'
The wind said, 'The Buddha statue is the greatest.'
And then I found out who is the greatest of all."
"Who is that?" Mother Mole asked.
"It is one of us, the moles!"
"Well, then, we must choose the best bridegroom from among the greatest moles," Mother replied.
As a result, Father Mole and Mother Mole met with Moler.
Soon, Mollie and Moler were married.
Couldn't the greatest in the world be right next to you?
Going on a bear hunt.
I'm not afraid.
It's a river.
It's a wide river.
We can't go over it.
We can't go under it.
Let's swim through it.
Going on a bear hunt.
I'm not afraid.
It's a tree.
It's a tall tree.
We can't go over it.
We can't go under it.
Let's climb up it.
Is there a bear over there?
No!
Is there a bear over there?
No!
Going on a bear hunt.
I'm not afraid.
It's grass. It's long grass.
We can't go over it.
We can't go under it.
Let's walk through it.
Going on a bear hunt.
I'm not afraid.
It's a cave.
It's a dark cave.
We can't go over it.
We can't go under it.
Let's creep inside.
Quiet.
Is there a bear in the cave?
YES, there is.
Run out of the cave.
Walk through the grass.
Climb up the tree and climb down the tree.
Swim through the river.
Go into the house and slam the door.
Jump into bed and pull up the covers.
"WE ARE NEVER GOING ON A BEAR HUNT AGAIN."
One winter it was very cold.
An old Japanese man named Yosaku and his wife, Ine, could find nothing to eat.
The snow was thick on the ground, and they had no money to buy food.
Yosaku was a very talented hat maker.
He usually sold his hats in the village.
But it was a cold, hard winter.
Because of the snow, the couple could not find grass to make hats.
One day, Yosaku and Ine searched through their food chests looking for rice.
Ine found only a few grains of rice left.
As she cooked the rice, some hungry mice came to watch.
Ine said, "Oh Yosaku, look! Even the poor mice are hungry.
It is a sad home that has hungry mice."
"Let us share our food with them, Ine," said Yosaku.
The mice were grateful.
"You are both so kind to us.
Usually people shoo mice away and we starve during the winter."
The mice ate the rice and, late during the night, snuck out into the cold snow.
The next morning, the mice surprised Yosaku and Ine.
All night long the brave mice had dug deep in the snow for precious grass.
They brought Yosaku and Ine enough grass for six hats.
"Look what gifts the mice have brought!
Now we can make grass hats for New Year's.
We can sell them in town and buy food!" said Yosaku.
Yosaku and Ine worked hard all that day.
They made six excellent hats to sell at the market.
As Yosaku walked to the market the next morning, he passed six Jizo-sama Buddhas.
Each Buddha had snow covering his head.
Yosaku felt sad at seeing this.
"I wish I could give an offering to you, Jizo-samas.
But sadly, I am only a poor hat maker."
Yosaku removed the towel from his head and wiped the snow off the Buddhas' heads.
At the market, Yosaku called out,
"Grass hats! Grass hats for sale for New Year's!"
But no one had money to buy his hats.
As Yosaku walked home, he passed the Jizo-sama Buddhas again.
"Oh, Jizo-samas!" he said, "I have not sold any hats, so I cannot give an offering of food to you.
But I will wipe the snow from your heads.
I will place my grass hats upon you so that you can stay warm at night."
The Jizo-samas remained silent, and Yosaku walked home.
The next morning was New Year's.
Yosaku and Ine woke to a cold room and a bare cupboard.
Their mice friends were also hungry and shivered in the corner.
Suddenly, there was a knock on the door.
Ine opened the door.
There stood the six Jizo-sama Buddhas.
In their outstretched hands were rice cakes, some vegetables, and the New Year's pine decoration.
One Jizo-sama said, "You have been good to Buddha.
You have helped the small animals and warmed us with your hats.
For this we honor you and give you New Year's offerings."
The Jizo-sama Buddhas bowed to Yosaku and Ine.
Yosaku and Ine began to cry with happiness.
To be honored by the Jizo-sama Buddhas was very unusual, and it was a special occasion.
They knew that the next year would be lucky for them and their friends.
Yosaku, Ine, and the mice crowded around the New Year's feast.
"Oh, how lucky we are to have friends and happiness, even at this cold New Year's celebration," said Yosaku.
Yosaku, his wife, and their mice friends enjoyed the heartwarming food from the Jizo-sama Buddhas.
"May we have a happy new year!" he said.

episodes.title: The Mayor and the Young Boy

subtitle.text: A very long time ago, there was a mean and corrupt mayor.
But his secretary was a kind man who hated injustice.
The mayor always felt nervous when his secretary was around.
His secretary was so kind and fair that the mayor could not do what he planned.
The mayor liked to be mean, but the secretary always asked him to change his decisions.
The mayor decided to find some fault with his secretary.
One day, during a terrible snowstorm, the mayor called his secretary into his office.
The mayor said with a cruel smile, "My good fellow, I have a desire for fresh peaches and strawberries.
I want you to go out and get these for me.
I know it is a difficult task, so I will give you one month to complete it."
Then he continued, "When you complete this task, I will reward you generously.
But if you should fail, I will ask you to resign."
The secretary didn't know how to refuse.
He thought to himself, "Where can I find peaches and strawberries at this time of year?
Nowhere! I couldn't even buy them with all the money in the world."
The mayor's demand was completely unreasonable.
But the secretary knew that the mayor was testing his loyalty.
"This is hopeless, totally hopeless," he moaned.
The secretary gathered his strength and decided to give the task his best try.
He told his family that he had to go away on important business.
He packed a small bag and set off in the snow to look for fresh peaches and strawberries.
He went from city to city but could not find the fruit anywhere.
After several weeks of searching, he became very sick and returned home.
The secretary's young son looked at him and asked, "Father, why did you go away?"
The sick father, fearing that he might die, told his son the truth.
The little boy listened quietly until his father finished.
Then he spoke:
"Father, I want you to rest and recover from your illness.
Please do not think about this task anymore.
I have an idea.
I think I can persuade the mayor to withdraw his demand."
The boy went to the mayor's house.
When the boy saw the mayor, he greeted him with a big bow and said,
"Your Honor, my father is seriously ill.
While he was out searching in the snow for fresh peaches and strawberries, he was bitten by a snake."
The mayor shook with anger.
"You disgusting liar!" he screamed. "You stupid child!
How could anyone be bitten by a snake in this cold weather?"
And he slammed his fist on the table.
The boy had expected this response.
He bowed and asked politely, "But Your Honor, if one cannot find a snake in this cold snow, how can one find fresh peaches and strawberries?"
The mayor was speechless.
The boy had tricked him.
He knew he had to withdraw his request.
When the town heard about what the mayor had done, they asked their king for a new mayor.
The king replaced the mean and corrupt mayor with the kind and fair secretary.
The new mayor ruled wisely, and his son received a great gift from the king.
Far away on the beautiful island of Hawaii, a powerful chief lived with his daughter.
She was a tropical princess, and they were happy on the island.
One day the princess became very ill from eating a spoiled mango.
The chief sent for the magical healer to save his daughter.
The healer shook his head sadly and said,
"There is only one thing that will save this girl.
You must find three golden flowers.
They grow where the glorious sun shines into sparkling water."
The chief wanted his daughter to stay alive, so he gathered all the men in the village.
He told them that whoever found the golden flowers could marry the princess.
Three brothers who lived across the river heard the chief's plea.
They were just poor farmers, but they knew their island paradise very well.
The brothers alone knew where to find the sacred healing flowers.
The first brother rowed his small boat, called a skiff, up the river.
He found the golden flowers by a sparkling waterfall.
He knew that only nine flowers grew in that special spot every year.
He took three of the magical flowers.
As he rowed back to the village, an old fisherman stopped him.
"What do you have there?" the fisherman asked.
The boy didn't trust the old man, so he answered, "Worms."
When the poor boy reached the village, he showed his basket to the chief.
But worms came out of his basket instead of the three golden flowers.
The next day, the very same thing happened to the second brother.
The chief was sad.
Then the third brother tried.
He was the youngest, kind in nature, and shy.
When the fisherman asked him what he had in the basket, he was honest.
He said, "I have three golden flowers."
The old fisherman looked in the basket and said, "So you do.
And you will need this flute."
The enchanted flowers cured the sick princess, but the chief went back on his promise.
He did not want a poor, simple farmer to marry his daughter.
The chief said, "Go out tonight with these one hundred birds.
If you can return in the morning with all one hundred birds, then you may marry my daughter."
But in the moonlight, the poor boy quickly lost all the birds.
Then he remembered the flute the fisherman had given him.
He played the mystical flute, and all the birds came back to him.
The chief was very surprised!
Had this poor farmer boy really charmed all one hundred birds?
He counted the birds twice.
Then the chief bowed his regal head and said,
"You will be a worthy husband for my daughter."
The poor farmer boy moved his whole family to the chief's village.
He lived there happily with his new wife.
And sometimes, early in the spring when the sun glinted off the sparkling waterfall,
the young man and his princess would watch the golden flowers shining by the waterfall.
Once upon a time, there was a widow and her son Jack.
They were very poor.
They lived in a little old house.
"Mom, I am hungry.
Can we eat something tonight?" asked Jack.
"Jack, we don't have any food left," his mother said.
"Tomorrow let's sell the cow.
She is too old to give milk.
You can take her to the market.
Sell her and buy some bread and meat."
"Yes, Mother," said Jack.
The next day, on the way to the market, Jack met a little old man.
"Sell me your cow," he said.
"I will give you this bean."
"No! How can that bean feed me and my mother?" said Jack.
"This bean is a magic bean.
It will grow a vine as high as the sky!
Up there is a magical kingdom with many wonderful things," said the old man.
"Wow!" thought Jack. "There might be food and money above the clouds."
So he sold the cow to the old man for the bean.
Jack was excited and hurried home.
"Jack, where are the bread and meat?" asked his mother.
"Look, Mother," said Jack.
"I sold the cow for a magic bean!"
"What? You fool! What can this bean do for us?
Now we will go hungry again tonight!"
And she threw the bean into the backyard.
The next morning, Jack looked outside.
"Mother, look! There is a huge beanstalk in our yard!"
"Oh! Take the ax and cut it down," his mother said.
But Jack believed the old man.
He climbed up the beanstalk, all the way to the top.
When he reached the top, he couldn't believe his eyes.
There was a huge castle in the clouds.
Jack knocked on the door.
A maid answered the door.
"Oh my, it's a little boy!
What are you doing here?"
"I wanted to see what was above the clouds," said Jack.
"Shh, be quiet!" the maid warned.
"My master, the giant, eats little children!
He's upstairs now. You must hide!"
"Did you say a giant lives here? Oh no!" said Jack.
"Yes! Quick, hide in the oven.
My master will come downstairs soon!"
Just as the maid pushed Jack into the oven, the giant arrived.
"Hmm, I smell a little boy!" said the giant.
"There is no one else here.
You are imagining things!" said the maid.
"Hmm, okay." The giant seemed satisfied.
"Bring me my goose then!" he ordered.
"Do you want your singing harp too?" asked the maid.
"Yes. Let the harp play some music while I count my golden eggs."
The giant sat at the table, and the maid brought the goose and the harp.
"Now, my goose, lay golden eggs for me. Ha-ha!" laughed the giant.
Jack watched through a hole in the oven door.
When he saw the goose lay a golden egg, he was amazed.
"Sniff, sniff! I still smell a child here," grumbled the giant.
"Hmm!" And the giant began to search everywhere.
Just as the giant was about to open the oven door, the maid shooed the magic goose away.
"Oh, master! The goose is flying away!"
The giant turned to look.
"What? Come back, goose!" he cried.
"Hurry, little boy! Get out of here quickly!" the maid told Jack.
But suddenly, the singing harp shouted out, "Stop! Who are you?
What are you doing here?"
"Shh!" said Jack.
But the harp didn't listen.
"Master, master! I found the child!
He's here!" called the harp.
"Ah-ha!" the giant roared.
"You will taste good for dinner!"
Quickly Jack escaped behind some jars.
The giant rushed to catch Jack, but he could not find him because Jack was so little.
"Oh, where are you, little boy? Come out!"
While the giant was searching for Jack, he slipped away and ran out of the castle as fast as he could.
"Oh, master! Look! He is running away," called the harp.
The giant chased after Jack.
But just as he was running out the castle door, the maid slammed the door on the giant's foot.
The giant tripped and fell down. "Ohh!"
When Jack reached the beanstalk, he saw the goose sitting on a cloud nearby.
"There's the goose!" he said.
Jack snatched it up and hurried down the beanstalk.
The giant ran to the beanstalk and started to climb down after Jack.
But he was not as quick, so Jack reached the ground first.
"Mom, Mom, quick! Where is the ax?" he cried.
"Jack, where have you been?
You left the ax right here," said his mom.
Jack grabbed the ax and started to cut down the beanstalk.
The beanstalk swayed back and forth as he chopped.
"Oh no! The beanstalk is going to fall!" cried the giant.
The giant held on as long as he could.
But soon he lost his grip and fell all the way down and died.
"Jack, what's going on here?" asked his mom.
"Mom, I climbed up to the top of the beanstalk.
Look what I found there.
This goose lays golden eggs!"
"Really? That's hard to believe!"
"Just watch! Lay some eggs!" he told the goose.
When his mother saw the large golden eggs, she was very pleased.
"Oh my goodness!"
After that, Jack and his mother were rich, and they were never hungry again.

episodes.title: Who is the King of the Forest?

subtitle.text: There was once a fox who lived in the forest.
He was a clever and cunning fox.
He could easily fool anyone.
One day, a tiger saw the fox and thought,
"He will make a tasty meal.
I will eat the little fox for dinner."
The tiger snuck up on the fox.
The tiger opened his mouth and was about to eat the fox.
But the fox yelled, "Stop! How dare you!
Do not touch me.
I am the King of the Forest."
The tiger stopped and chuckled.
"Ha-ha! You? You are not the King of the Forest.
You are just a small, silly fox."
The fox knew he was not the King of the Forest, but he planned to trick the tiger.
"I am! I'm the King of the Forest.
And I can prove it."
"You are not the King of the Forest.
All I see is a little fox," said the tiger.
The fox thought quickly.
Because he was very clever, he soon had a plan.
"Truly, I am the King of the Forest.
When the other animals see me, they run away."
"They run away from you?
Ha-ha-ha! No one runs away from you.
You are a silly, skinny fox," laughed the tiger.
The fox knew that the deer were afraid of the tiger.
So he said, "Let's go see the deer.
They will run away."
The fox and the tiger went to see the deer.
When the deer saw the tiger, they ran away.
"Run, run! It is the King of the Forest," cried the deer.
"Look at them.
They are afraid of me.
I am the King of the Forest," said the fox.
"Hmm? I still don't believe you.
You are just a little fox," the tiger said.
"Let's go see the monkeys.
They will run away too," said the fox.
So the fox and the tiger went to see the monkeys.
When the monkeys saw the tiger, they ran away.
"Swing, swing! It's the King of the Forest," they said.
"They are afraid of you!" the tiger said.
"Of course they are.
I am the King of the Forest.
All animals are afraid of me," boasted the fox.
The tiger believed the fox.
Now he was afraid of the fox too.
"I am so sorry, my great king.
Please do not hurt me!"
"I will let you go, but you must never try to hurt me again," said the fox.
The tiger thanked the fox and bowed to him.
"My king, I will never hurt you again.
You are a furious, furry fox."
"You may go," said the fox smiling.
That night, the fox told all his friends about the tiger.
The fox and his friends laughed and laughed.
Long ago, there lived a farmer and his dog named Shelly.
The dog was very faithful to his master.
The farmer also liked the dog very much.
He took good care of his dog.
One hot day, the farmer returned home from the field.
"Whew! I am thirsty!
I wonder where the water jar is," he said.
He found the jar and lifted it to drink some water.
But all of a sudden, the dog barked.
"Woof, woof."
The dog barked and barked some more.
"Oh, Shelly! Please be quiet!" the farmer said.
"Are you thirsty too?
I will give you some water when I am finished."
But the dog did not stop barking.
He even jumped up on his master.
"Hmm," said the farmer.
"Maybe, you are hungry.
Let me drink some water first.
Then I will give you something to eat."
"Woof, woof, woof!" barked the dog.
"Oh, what's the matter with you?
You are so greedy!
Can't you let me drink some water first?"
The farmer was so angry that he kicked his dog!
But the dog did not stop jumping on him.
"You are crazy, Shelly!
Go away!" said the farmer.
The dog did not give up.
He jumped up and bit his master's hand.
"Ouch!" yelled the farmer.
The jar crashed on the ground and broke into pieces.
"Oh no!" The farmer was so angry that he picked up a stick to hit the dog.
But then he noticed a dead snake among the pieces of the jar.
He knew that the snake was poisonous.
"Oh my! Then the water is poisonous too!" said the farmer.
"Hmm, I guess Shelly saw the snake slip into the jar."
"Woof, woof!" Shelly barked and wagged his tail.
"Oh, my faithful dog!
You saved my life!"
The farmer felt sorry and regretted hurting his dog.
He gave Shelly a pat.
"You were right, Shelly.
Next time, I will listen!
And I promise not to hit you ever again," he said.
Long ago, a rich man lived in a small village with his son.
The father had to send his son to school far away from home.
"Son," he said, "you will receive a good education at this school."
So the son went away to study.
The father was very sad, but he believed it would be worth it.
Someday his son would come back as a successful and well-educated man.
A few years later, the father became very sick.
He called his servant, "Come here.
I want you to write down my will.
I might not be able to see my son again."
"Yes, master." The servant obeyed.
"To you, my servant, I will give all of my money and my lands.
To my son, I will give one thing only, but he may choose what he will ask for.
Please deliver this will to my son."
"Of course, master," said the servant.
Then the father died.
"Ha-ha! All he had is now mine." The servant laughed.
He was so pleased that he hurried to the son and gave him the letter from his dead father.
"Oh no! Father!" cried the son.
Days passed, and the son was sad and puzzled.
He did not understand why his father had left everything to the servant, but only one request to him.
"Why did my father give everything to his servant? Why?"
The son consulted his wise teacher about this.
"Teacher, I never hurt my father and always tried to obey him.
I thought he loved me.
But I guess he did not love me after all."
"Wait, don't think like that," answered the teacher.
"He really was a very wise father!"
"What? I don't understand," said the son.
The teacher explained:
"After your father died, you said that there was no one in the house besides the servant."
"Yes!" said the son.
"Then, after he died, what if the servant had run away with all of your father's treasures?
Your father must have worried about this.
So he told the servant that everything would belong to him.
That way, his servant was pleased to come and tell you about your father's death."
"But what good does it do me?
Father's servant owns everything now!" complained the son.
"Think about it a bit more," suggested the teacher.
"Remember that every servant's possessions belong to his master.
Doesn't your father's will say that you can ask for one thing?"
"Yes!"
"So ask your father's servant to be your servant.
Then everything of your father's will belong to you!"
"Ah!" cried the son.
"Now I understand how wise my father was!
I must go back home right away."
He thanked his teacher and left.
When he returned home, he met his father's servant.
"I am here to make my one request," he said.
"Okay," replied the servant.
"According to your father's will, you can ask for only one thing."
"My only request is that you serve me for the rest of your life."
"What? No way!" said the servant.
But deep down inside his heart, the servant knew that a servant's possessions belong to his master.
He could not refuse the son's request.
"Do not feel so sad," said the son.
"I will share my wealth with you."
"Oh, thank you! I will serve you gladly!" replied the servant.
The son was proud to be the son of such a wise man.
So he tried to become just like his father.
He treated his servant very well.
Eventually, the son also became a wise and successful businessman, just like his father.
